questions.stem: Almost all surviving Greek and Roman literature about women was written by men of the elite. What is the main consequence for historians?
options: Sources describe only enslaved women, since elite women were never mentioned
Sources were written by women under male names, so they are fully balanced
Sources show ideals and male attitudes more than women's own experiences
Sources are unreliable on every topic, so they cannot be used at all
questions.explanation: Male authors often described how women ought to behave, so texts reveal attitudes and ideals more than lived reality. Historians balance them with inscriptions, papyri and archaeology rather than discarding them.

questions.stem: Under Roman law in the Republic, a free woman could NOT:
options: vote in the assemblies or hold office
inherit property from her father's estate
dine with her husband and his male guests
attend religious festivals and the games
questions.explanation: Roman women were excluded from voting and public office, but they could inherit and own property, usually with a guardian's approval. Unlike respectable Athenian women, they could dine with guests and attend festivals and spectacles.

questions.stem: Augustus gave freeborn Roman women who had borne three children the right to manage their own affairs without a guardian (the ius trium liberorum). What was the main aim of this reward?
options: To free all enslaved women who became mothers
To stop women from owning any land in Italy
To encourage elite families to have more children
To allow women to stand for election to the Senate
questions.explanation: Augustus was worried by low birth rates among the elite and rewarded marriage and children while penalising the unmarried. The privilege freed mothers from guardianship but gave no political rights.

questions.stem: Compared with women in classical Athens, women in New Kingdom Egypt had greater legal rights. Which right did Egyptian women have?
options: They could vote in the assembly alongside the men of their town
They could serve as soldiers in the army on the same terms as men
They could inherit the throne automatically as the eldest child
They could own property, make contracts and bring cases to court
questions.explanation: Egyptian documents show women buying and selling property, making wills and appearing in court in their own right, while Athenian women needed a male guardian (kyrios). Egypt had no voting assembly, and the throne normally passed to a son.

questions.stem: In Egyptian tomb paintings, men are usually painted with reddish-brown skin and women with paler, yellowish skin. Historians usually interpret this as:
options: a sign that women were forbidden by law to leave the house in daylight
the result of different paints fading at different rates over time
a convention linking men with outdoor work and women with the home
proof that men and women in Egypt came from different ethnic groups
questions.explanation: The colours followed a convention of ideal gender roles, with men shown as active outdoors and women as belonging to the household. Other evidence shows women working in fields and markets, so the convention is not a literal record.

questions.stem: The Vestal Virgins served the goddess Vesta in Rome for thirty years. They were freed from their fathers' authority, could make wills and had special seats at the games, yet faced death if they broke their vow of chastity. What does this best show about women in Roman religious life?
options: Some women gained high status because their role protected the state
Women controlled Roman religion, since all priesthoods were held by women
Roman women had full equality with men once they became priestesses
Religious roles were a punishment given to women who refused to marry
questions.explanation: The Vestals' privileges came from their task of keeping the sacred fire, on which Rome's safety was thought to depend, and the harsh penalty shows how closely their purity was tied to the state. Most priesthoods were held by men.

questions.stem: During Rome's wars of expansion in the second and first centuries BCE, the largest source of new slaves was:
options: prisoners of war from conquered lands
Roman citizens sold for unpaid debts
volunteers who sold themselves for wages
criminals sentenced by the courts in Rome
questions.explanation: Conquests in Greece, Spain, North Africa and Gaul brought huge numbers of captives to Italy. Debt bondage of citizens had been abolished in the early Republic, and convicts were a minor source.

questions.stem: Why is it hard for historians to study the experience of enslaved people in Greece and Rome?
options: Enslaved people wrote long memoirs that were later lost in fires
Archaeology cannot find any trace of the places where slaves worked
Most surviving texts were written by owners, not the enslaved
Slavery was so rare that it is hardly mentioned in any source
questions.explanation: Writers such as Cato, Varro and Seneca wrote as owners, so the voices of the enslaved survive mainly in short epitaphs and inscriptions. Slavery was widespread, and archaeology does reveal mines, workshops and slave quarters.

questions.stem: Aristotle argued in the Politics that some people are slaves by nature. This view is best used by historians as evidence of:
options: an elite Greek justification for the practice of slavery
the official law code of Athens on how to treat slaves
the opinions held by most enslaved people in Greece
a campaign by Greek philosophers to abolish slavery
questions.explanation: Aristotle's theory shows how some educated Greeks justified slavery, often linking it with non-Greeks. It is not a law code, and it tells us nothing directly about what the enslaved themselves thought.

questions.stem: A Roman slave who was formally freed by a citizen owner became a citizen, but could not hold public office, while his freeborn son could. What does this show about Roman attitudes to slavery?
options: Freed slaves had higher status than freeborn citizens because of their hard work
Romans rejected slavery and freed every slave after a fixed period of service
Slavery was a status one could leave, though its stain lasted a generation
Romans believed slavery was natural and permanent, so no one was ever freed
questions.explanation: Manumission was common in Rome and freedmen could become rich, as their tombs show, but they kept obligations to their former owners and some legal limits. Their children were freeborn, which shows that the stigma faded over a generation.

questions.stem: The revolt led by Spartacus, which began in 73 BCE, started when:
options: rowers on the Roman fleet seized their warships
miners at Laurion attacked their Athenian guards
helots rose against Sparta after an earthquake
gladiators broke out of a training school at Capua
questions.explanation: Spartacus and fellow gladiators escaped from a school at Capua and gathered a large army of runaway slaves that defeated several Roman forces. Crassus crushed the revolt in 71 BCE, and captured rebels were crucified along the Appian Way.

questions.stem: The Parthenon in Athens was built mainly in which order of Greek architecture?
options: Tuscan
Composite
Doric
Corinthian
questions.explanation: The Parthenon's columns are Doric, though the building also has an Ionic frieze. The Corinthian order was developed later and used widely by the Romans, who also created the Composite and Tuscan forms.

questions.stem: Traces of pigment show that Greek marble statues and temples were originally brightly painted. Why does this matter for historians?
options: It shows the Greeks had no interest in sculpture, only in painted pottery
It means the statues were made of plaster and painted to look like marble
The white marble image of Greek art comes from the loss of its original colour
It proves the statues were made by Roman copyists rather than by Greek artists
questions.explanation: Weathering removed most of the paint, and later artists admired the plain white marble they saw, so the modern image of classical art differs from what ancient viewers saw. Surviving sources can mislead if their condition is not considered.

questions.stem: Roman builders could roof large spaces such as the Pantheon in Rome mainly because they used:
options: timber trusses and thatched roofing
stone columns set very close together
concrete and the arch, vault and dome
iron beams and plate-glass windows
questions.explanation: Roman concrete could be poured into curved forms, allowing arches, vaults and domes that spanned large interiors without many supports. The Pantheon's dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

questions.stem: Egyptian artists usually drew a person with the head and legs in profile but the eye and shoulders seen from the front. The main reason was that:
options: the style was copied from Greek vase painters of the classical period
each part was shown from its clearest angle, following set rules
Egyptian artists had not yet discovered how to draw a face in profile
the figures were meant to be read as several different people at once
questions.explanation: Egyptian art aimed to show each part of the body clearly and completely, following a canon of proportions, rather than to copy what the eye saw from one position. The style is far older than classical Greece.

questions.stem: The tomb of the baker and contractor Marcus Vergilius Eurysaces in Rome is decorated with a frieze showing bread being made. Why is it useful for studying Roman art?
options: It is the only surviving Roman monument that shows people at work
It shows a non-elite patron using art to display his trade and wealth
It shows that only senators were allowed to build decorated tombs in Rome
It proves that Roman art was made only to honour the gods and the emperor
questions.explanation: Wealthy non-elite Romans, many of them freedmen, often chose monuments that celebrated the work that had made them rich, unlike senators, who stressed office and ancestry. This shows that art was used by groups beyond the ruling elite.

questions.stem: Buddhist sculpture from Gandhara, in modern Pakistan and Afghanistan, shows the Buddha with wavy hair and draped robes in a Greek style. This is evidence of:
options: the spread of Hellenistic art after Alexander's conquests
Buddhist monks travelling to Athens to train as sculptors
Roman emperors ordering the Buddha to be shown as a god
Egyptian sculptors settling in India under the Pharaohs
questions.explanation: Greek rulers and settlers remained in Bactria and north-western India after Alexander, and their artistic styles blended with Buddhist subjects. Gandharan art is a clear example of the spread of art forms through cultural contact.

questions.stem: The hoplite phalanx of classical Greece relied above all on:
options: fast-moving horse archers who attacked the enemy from long distance
war elephants charging ahead of lightly armed infantry
small groups of soldiers fighting separately in rough country
a close formation of men shielding each other with round shields
questions.explanation: Hoplites stood shoulder to shoulder, each partly covered by his neighbour's shield (the hoplon), so the line was strong only while it held together. Horse archers were typical of steppe peoples and Persians, not Greek hoplites.

questions.stem: The main weapon of a Greek trireme in battle was:
options: a large sail that let it outrun enemy ships
a bronze ram on the bow, driven by its rowers
a catapult on the deck that threw burning stones
rows of archers firing from high wooden towers
questions.explanation: The trireme was a light, fast warship rowed by about 170 men in three tiers, which tried to ram and hole enemy ships. Its sails were used for travel, not battle.

questions.stem: In the manipular legion of the middle Republic, soldiers were arranged in three lines: hastati, principes and triarii. How were these lines organised?
options: By weapon, with archers at the front and swordsmen at the back
By age and experience, with the veterans in the rear line
By wealth, with the richest men fighting on horseback at the front
By homeland, with each line made up of one Italian people
questions.explanation: The younger hastati fought first, then the principes in their prime, and the veteran triarii formed the last reserve. Wealth decided who served as cavalry, but the three infantry lines were based on age and experience.

questions.stem: At Cannae in 216 BCE, Hannibal let his centre fall back while his African infantry and cavalry closed in on the Roman flanks and rear. Why is the battle studied as a key military encounter?
options: It ended the Second Punic War with the capture of the city of Rome
Roman war elephants won the battle by charging through the centre
It was the first battle in which the Romans used the hoplite phalanx
A smaller army encircled and destroyed a larger one
questions.explanation: Hannibal's outnumbered army encircled the Romans and inflicted one of the worst defeats in Roman history. Rome refused to surrender, however, and won the war at Zama in 202 BCE.

questions.stem: Wooden writing tablets found at the fort of Vindolanda, near Hadrian's Wall in northern Britain, are especially valuable for studying the Roman army because they:
options: list the names of every soldier who served in the Roman army
record daily life, supplies and letters at a frontier fort
contain the official battle plans for the conquest of Britain
were written by Celtic warriors describing their raids on Rome
questions.explanation: The tablets include strength reports, requests for supplies and leave, and private letters, such as a birthday invitation between officers' wives. They give a rare view of everyday service rather than famous battles.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes an impact of Roman conquest on the conquered?
options: Conquered peoples kept their armies and paid nothing to Rome
Rome forced every province to give up its own gods and language
Many were enslaved or taxed, but local elites could gain citizenship and office
All conquered people were made full citizens on the day of their defeat
questions.explanation: Conquest brought enslavement, tribute and Roman garrisons, but Rome also drew provincial elites into its system through citizenship and local government. Rome generally tolerated local religions and languages.

questions.stem: In the Egyptian Book of the Dead, the judgement of the deceased involved:
options: weighing the heart against the feather of Ma'at
crossing a river by paying a coin to Charon
being buried with a horse for the journey west
burning the body to free the soul from the flesh
questions.explanation: The heart was weighed against the feather of Ma'at in front of Osiris; a heart heavy with wrongdoing was eaten by the monster Ammit. Paying Charon belongs to Greek belief.

questions.stem: Greeks sometimes placed a coin, often an obol, with the dead. The purpose was to:
options: pay the priests who carried out the funeral ceremony
pay Charon to ferry the soul across into the underworld
buy food for the dead person at festivals in their honour
show the family's wealth to the gods of Mount Olympus
questions.explanation: In Greek belief Charon ferried souls across the river into Hades, and the coin was his fare. The custom is known from literature and from coins found in graves, though not every burial included one.

questions.stem: Roman law from the Twelve Tables onwards required that the dead be buried or cremated outside the city walls. As a result, Roman cemeteries were usually found:
options: inside the courtyards of private houses
on islands set aside for the dead in rivers
lining the roads leading out of the city
beneath the floors of temples in the forum
questions.explanation: Tombs lined roads such as the Appian Way outside Rome, where passers-by could read epitaphs and remember the dead. Burial inside the city was forbidden, with rare exceptions.

questions.stem: Polybius describes Roman noble funerals in which men wore wax masks (imagines) of the family's ancestors who had held high office. What was the main purpose of this custom?
options: To hide the faces of mourners from evil spirits during the rites
To show that all Roman citizens were equal in death
To scare away thieves from robbing the tomb after burial
To display the family's history of service and inspire the young
questions.explanation: The masks paraded the family's consuls and other office-holders, linking the dead to a line of famous ancestors and urging young men to match them. The custom stressed noble rank, not equality.

questions.stem: The Hochdorf grave in southern Germany, found intact, held a Celtic chieftain of the Hallstatt period on a bronze couch with a wagon, drinking horns and a large Greek bronze cauldron. What does it best show?
options: A wealthy elite with long-distance contacts, buried ready to feast
That the Celts cremated all their dead and left no grave goods behind
That Celtic chieftains were buried in pyramids copied from Egypt
That the Greeks ruled southern Germany during the Hallstatt period
questions.explanation: The rich goods and feasting equipment point to an elite whose status was shown by hospitality, and the Greek cauldron shows trade with the Mediterranean. Because it was unlooted, the grave gives rare complete evidence.

questions.stem: Painted Etruscan tombs at Tarquinia show banquets, music and dancing, and the terracotta Sarcophagus of the Spouses shows a husband and wife reclining together. Greek writers were shocked that Etruscan women dined with men. What can a historian best conclude?
options: The Greek writers must be wrong, since tomb paintings always show reality
Etruscan elite women shared social life more openly than Greek women did
Etruscan women ruled the cities, so men appear only as servants in tombs
Etruscans believed in no afterlife, so they painted only scenes of daily life
questions.explanation: The tomb art and the Greek criticism agree that elite Etruscan women dined publicly with men, which Greek custom forbade for respectable wives. Tomb scenes are idealised and may show the afterlife banquet, so they need care.

questions.stem: Most of the best-known burials from the ancient world, such as royal tombs and noble graves, belonged to the wealthy. What is the main problem this creates for studying funerary customs?
options: The customs of ordinary people are under-represented in the evidence
No graves of the wealthy have survived, so only the poor can be studied
Elite tombs were all looted, so they contain no information at all
Ordinary people were never buried, so there is nothing to compare
questions.explanation: Simple graves leave fewer and less durable remains and attract less excavation, so knowledge of death customs is tilted towards the elite. Even looted tombs still give evidence through their architecture and art.

questions.stem: Darius I's inscription at Behistun, carved high on a cliff in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, tells how he defeated rebels with the favour of Ahuramazda. What was its main purpose?
options: To record the laws of Persia for judges in every province
To mark the border between the Persian Empire and Greece
To honour the rebels as brave men who fought for freedom
To justify Darius's right to rule after a disputed succession
questions.explanation: Darius came to power after a crisis over the throne, and the inscription presents him as the god's chosen king and his rivals as liars. Its three languages later helped scholars decipher cuneiform.

questions.stem: Reliefs on the Apadana staircase at Persepolis show rows of delegates from across the empire bringing gifts to the king. What image of power do they present?
options: A king defeated in battle forced to pay tribute to the Greeks
A democratic assembly in which each people votes on the law
A temple procession of priests offering gifts to Egyptian gods
A vast, orderly empire whose peoples willingly honour the king
questions.explanation: The delegates walk calmly with their gifts rather than appearing as defeated captives, presenting the empire as peaceful and united under the king. The reliefs are royal propaganda, not a neutral record of how the provinces felt.

questions.stem: Egyptian kings were often shown grasping a kneeling enemy by the hair and raising a mace to strike him. This 'smiting scene' was meant to show the king as:
options: a peacemaker who refused to fight against his neighbours
a priest leading the daily offering rites in the temple
a servant of the foreign rulers who controlled Egypt
the defender of order against chaos and foreign enemies
questions.explanation: The smiting scene, used for thousands of years, presented the king as the upholder of Ma'at who crushed chaos, often shown as foreigners. It was a conventional image, not always a record of a real battle.

questions.stem: Roman emperors' portraits and slogans appeared on coins used across the empire. Why are coins valuable sources for the image of authority figures?
options: They were minted by the emperor's enemies to criticise his rule
They give an unbiased account of the emperor's private life
They show the messages a ruler chose to spread to his subjects
They record exactly what ordinary people thought of each emperor
questions.explanation: Coin designs, chosen by the ruler or his officials, advertised victories, virtues and heirs to people throughout the empire. They reveal the intended image, not public opinion or the truth of the ruler's character.

questions.stem: A young Roman noble of the late Republic typically served as a military officer before standing for quaestor, praetor and consul, and consuls commanded armies. What does this show about the ruling elite?
options: Generals were forbidden by law from taking part in politics
Only soldiers who rose from the ranks could become senators
Political and military leadership were held by the same men
The army chose all magistrates without any vote of the people
questions.explanation: The cursus honorum combined civil office and military command, so a senator's career depended on success in war as well as in the assemblies. Magistrates were elected, and nobles started as officers rather than rising from the ranks.

questions.stem: The Uluburun shipwreck, found off the southern coast of Turkey and dated to about the late fourteenth century BCE, carried about ten tonnes of copper and one tonne of tin. Why is this cargo significant?
options: It proves the Bronze Age ended because the ship's copper never reached its buyers
It shows that iron had already replaced bronze for weapons across the Aegean
It shows that only one kingdom, Egypt, traded by sea in the Late Bronze Age
The ten-to-one mix matches bronze, showing trade in its raw materials
questions.explanation: Bronze is roughly nine or ten parts copper to one part tin, so the ship carried enough metal to make about eleven tonnes of bronze. With goods from Egypt, Cyprus, the Levant and the Aegean, it shows a wide network of trade.

questions.stem: The Phoenicians, based in cities such as Tyre and Sidon, were famous for producing:
options: purple dye made from murex sea snails
silk woven from the cocoons of moths
porcelain fired at very high heat
papyrus made from Nile reeds
questions.explanation: Tyrian purple, extracted from murex shellfish, was so costly that it became a colour of royalty. Silk and porcelain came from China, and papyrus from Egypt.

questions.stem: The Greek alphabet was adapted in the eighth century BCE from the script of the Phoenicians. This is an example of:
options: a script forced on the Greeks by conquest
an invention made separately with no contact
a writing system copied from Egyptian priests
cultural exchange carried along trade routes
questions.explanation: Greeks in contact with Phoenician traders borrowed their letters and added vowels, creating an alphabet that spread through the Mediterranean. The Phoenicians never conquered Greece.

questions.stem: Roman pottery and amphorae have been excavated at Arikamedu in southern India, and Pliny the Elder complained that Rome's money was draining away to the East for luxuries. What do these sources together best show?
options: Rome conquered southern India and built a colony there for veterans
Indian merchants controlled the city of Rome and its grain supply
Romans had no interest in goods from beyond the Mediterranean
Trade with India was large enough to be noticed and criticised in Rome
questions.explanation: The archaeological finds confirm Roman goods reached India, while Pliny's complaint shows elite unease about spending on spices, pearls and silks. Rome never ruled India; Greek and Roman ships used the monsoon winds to sail there and back.

questions.stem: Herodotus devoted a whole book of his Histories to Egypt, describing its customs, religion and monuments. As evidence of Greek attitudes to other cultures, it shows:
options: a Persian report on the provinces of the empire
curiosity and respect mixed with misunderstanding
a complete rejection of everything that was not Greek
an Egyptian priest's own account of his religion
questions.explanation: Herodotus admired Egypt's age and wisdom and recorded what he saw and heard, but he also repeated mistaken stories and judged customs by Greek standards. He wrote as a Greek visitor, not as an Egyptian or Persian official.
